Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 76
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Mechanic
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Earth/Outdoor): Soil or outdoor smells, Stress: Stress, Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

Vignette:
Malee Srisombat is a 76-year-old Thai American woman who has worked as a mechanic at a small family-owned auto shop for over three decades. She came to the clinic accompanied by her husband, who sat quietly in the waiting room while she spoke, and who had, according to Malee, been urging her for months to talk to someone. Her PCL-5 score of 56 places her firmly in the severe range, and the picture that emerged across the intake and first two sessions was of a woman whose sense of safety had been methodically dismantled over the course of a prolonged stalking campaign and had never fully been rebuilt.

Approximately two years ago, a former customer at the auto shop began returning with increasing frequency — not for repairs, but to watch her. At first Malee dismissed it. She had spent her life in a garage, had learned to read engines and men with equal pragmatism. But the visits escalated. He began appearing at the end of her street in the early mornings when she walked to work, standing near the chain-link fence that borders the lot's side entrance, which runs along a strip of unpaved ground where weeds grow thick. She remembers the smell of that earth on one particular morning — damp, loamy, faintly organic — when she looked up from beneath a truck's undercarriage and saw him standing just beyond the fence, watching her in silence. He said nothing. He simply stood there. That smell, she has come to understand, is now inseparable from the sensation of being seen without her consent. On damp mornings when the soil around the shop releases that same odor, something in her body responds before her mind has caught up.

The stalking continued for several months before he was formally warned by police. During that period, Malee had no language for what was happening to her internally. She kept working, kept showing up, kept torquing bolts and reading diagnostic codes. But something had shifted. She had come to believe, in a way she could not fully articulate, that no space was truly sealed against intrusion — not the shop, not the street, not her own home. Even now, inside the house she has shared with her husband for forty years, she finds herself listening for sounds that should not be there, checking that the back door is locked two and three times before bed, scanning the windows when headlights pass. The feeling of being watched has not departed with the man who caused it.

At work, the consequences have been concrete and accumulating. Malee used to take quiet pride in training younger mechanics, in the unhurried concentration that made her good at her job. Now she frequently stops mid-task to look behind her toward the shop's open bay doors, a habit her coworkers have noticed and, with the kindness of people who do not know what to say, have stopped mentioning. She has begun avoiding the side lot entirely, routing herself through the front entrance even when it adds ten minutes to her morning. A junior mechanic now handles jobs near the fence line without knowing why she has stopped taking them.

What makes Malee's presentation particularly striking is the quality of her memory for the event and the way she speaks about it — or, more precisely, the way she cannot. When she attempts to describe the worst moments of the stalking, she loses the thread mid-sentence, her voice trailing into silence while her eyes move as though tracking something across the middle distance. At other moments, she describes specific images with an almost eerie precision — the exact pattern of light on the fence, the angle of his shoulders — as though she is reading from photographs she did not choose to take. She has also noticed that when the memory begins to surface fully, she pushes it away before it can complete itself, preferring the blankness to whatever comes next.

What finally brought her in was a Saturday afternoon when she had been sitting in the garden with her husband, the air warm, her body briefly at ease — and found herself suddenly certain that something terrible was about to happen. The happiness itself had felt like a warning. She told her husband that evening that she was tired of being afraid of feeling safe. That is what she most hopes to recover: not the absence of fear exactly, but the ability to sit in her own garden without her body treating peace as a trap.
